title: The Garden next door
hook: Epicurus taught in a garden: simple pleasures, friends, and freedom from fear (Diogenes Laërtius 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Crates and Hipparchia, a proposal with nothing to offer but a cloak, and a woman arguing as an equal. Your line was as an equal. Where did you speak up? Day six hundred fifty.

Say the word epicurean today and people picture a tasting menu: truffles, a wine list, a chef with tweezers. The man the word comes from would have been baffled. He lived very plainly and thought a little pot of cheese was a feast. And while the Stoics were arguing in a busy public porch in the middle of Athens, he and his friends were outside the city walls, in a garden. Two schools, same city, same century, very different answers. Today: the Garden next door.
screen: `EPICUREAN: A TASTING MENU?` → `A POT OF CHEESE WAS A FEAST.` → `THE GARDEN OUTSIDE THE WALLS.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Epicurus came to Athens around 306 BC and bought a garden, just outside the city. His school became known simply as the Garden, the way Zeno's became the Porch. It was more like a community than a lecture hall. Friends lived and ate together, and Diogenes Laërtius names women and at least one enslaved man among the circle, which was unusual for a school of philosophy. Second, the goal. Epicurus taught that the aim of life is pleasure. That's the word that scandalized people then and misleads people now. He meant something quiet: no pain in the body, and no turmoil in the mind. The Greek for that inner calm is ataraxia, being untroubled. He thought most of our misery comes from wanting things we don't need and fearing things we needn't fear. Third, the fears. The two big ones, he said, are fear of the gods and fear of death. Epicureans held that the gods exist but don't punish or meddle, and that the world is made of atoms moving in the void, so death is simply the end of feeling. The Stoics disagreed sharply, believing in a providential reason running through all things. Both schools sought a calm mind; they drew different maps to it, and each had thoughtful followers for centuries. Fourth, the heart of the Garden: friends. Simple food, shared. Conversation. People who know you. For Epicurus, that was not a side dish to the good life. It was most of the meal.
screen: `A GARDEN OUTSIDE ATHENS.` · `PLEASURE MEANS QUIET, NOT LUXURY.` · `NO FEAR OF GODS OR DEATH.` · `FRIENDS ARE MOST OF THE MEAL.` · then, large: `THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one simple pleasure you could share with a friend this week. Not an event. Something small: a coffee on a bench, a walk around the block, a bowl of soup, a phone call while you both fold laundry. Picture the friend. Picture the place. Notice whether the pleasure needs anything you don't already have. Usually it doesn't. Let yourself feel, ahead of time, how good it will be. The bell holds the time.
The Garden next door. Epicurus's school, outside Athens: simple pleasures, friends, and freedom from fear of the gods and death. Today's word.
Your line: the garden. Send one message today inviting a friend to your simple pleasure, and put it on the calendar. Day six hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Epicureans, ancient and modern, practice a simple life centered on friendship, modest pleasures and freedom from fear, often gathering to share plain meals and conversation.

a garden outside the city, with friends living together.
fork.reveal: Epicurus bought a garden outside the walls, and his school became a community of friends: the Garden.

original.note: Greek: garden. The name of Epicurus's school, as the Stoa (porch) named Zeno's.

trapdoor: what you thought: epicurean means a lover of gourmet food.
what it means: Epicurus taught a quiet pleasure: friends, simple things, and freedom from fear.
what a scholar hears: Epicurean hēdonē is defined mainly negatively, as aponia and ataraxia; Diogenes Laërtius book ten preserves three of Epicurus's letters and the Principal Doctrines.

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Epicurus 341–270 BC; arrived in Athens and bought the garden c. 307/306 BC. Confirm.
Pot of cheese: Epicurus asks a friend to send a little pot of cheese so he can feast when he likes (DL 10.11). Bread and water: same passage. Confirm.
Women in the circle (Leontion, Themista and others) and Mys, an enslaved man Epicurus freed in his will (DL 10.21). Confirm.
The garden lay outside the city walls, near the Dipylon gate road toward the Academy; some scholars place it inside. Hedge if needed.
Stoic and Epicurean views presented side by side without ranking.
